title: Training an LLM from Scratch, Locally — Angelos Perivolaropoulos, ElevenLabs
talk_summary: A hands-on workshop on training a tiny GPT-2-style character-level LLM from scratch in PyTorch on a laptop or free Colab T4, covering tokenizer choice, transformer blocks, training loop, learning-rate schedule, and sampling. It is an educational ML-fundamentals talk, not about agent orchestration or production LLM systems.

takeaways.technique: Held-out validation loss as cheap overfit/regression signal
takeaways.what_they_do: They split data into train and validation, run a forward pass on unseen data each eval interval, and treat rising val loss while train loss falls as overfitting; they also flag loss spikes as bugs.
takeaways.numbers: val loss optimum around 2,400 steps; below ~1.0 loss overfitting begins

takeaways.technique: Match tokenizer/model size to data and task budget
takeaways.what_they_do: They argue tokenizer and model size must match available data and compute; a too-large vocab or context never converges on limited data, so they pick the smallest viable configuration and scale only when data supports it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if we did try to train using a full tokenizer, this will never converge
takeaways.numbers: 65-token char vocab vs 50k GPT-2 vocab; 1.8M-param model

takeaways.technique: Context window sized to task, not maximized
takeaways.what_they_do: They stress that increasing context length is not a free parameter: it must be matched by architecture and data or training goes out of memory/unstable, and they use a deliberately small 256-token window for the toy task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You can't just change this number. You have to change the architecture
takeaways.numbers: 256-token block size vs 16k common, 1M in big labs

takeaways.what_they_do: The training loop saves a checkpoint every N steps and runs inference on the current checkpoint so a run can be resumed from the last good state instead of restarting.
takeaways.evidence_quote: every 1,000 steps, you save your checkpoint to be able to restart your training if you need it from that point

takeaways.what_they_do: They explain that seeds make sampling deterministic so a given prompt+seed reproduces the same output, and recommend using a seed even with greedy decoding because hidden randomness can remain.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you use a a set seed then your inference will always be returning the same value

takeaways.what_they_do: They describe a two-tier labeling org: senior labelers produce gold data and promoted QA labelers audit entry-level output, with accountability for QA quality.
